rv.q: Icke stunningly and elegantly opens up the closed worlds of the observer and the observed depicted in the film.

So it's fitting that Robert Icke 's ingenious staging of the 2006. German espionage thriller The Lives of Others feels like a vast act of transfiguration – turning grimy state machinery into heartstopping visual poetry.
And the achievement of the production, played without interval and often using a stage revolve to create a sense of remorseless scrutiny, is that it has its own strange, nightmarish logic.

As the adaptor and director, he imposes his aesthetic on every aspect of the evening — as he did in his recent update of Oedipus — but in the end you are often left admiring the bravura flourishes rather than being drawn into the story itself.
Slickly staged, but emotionally subdued story of state surveillance from acclaimed director Robert Icke
But to me, this does not manage the immensely difficult task it sets itself.

Dillane imbues the character with a blankly unemotional obedience to the Stasi cause, which eventually cracks as he is exposed to the couple's lives, personalities and the reality of what he is committed his life to becomes all too clear.

As the flat turns, events unfold inside it and Wiesler, at first sitting to one side, earphones clamped to his head, typing his impersonal reports – “unwrap presents, then have intercourse” – becomes changed by them.
The director/designer pairing is infused with an innate mutual understanding and their execution here is a finely orchestrated gem.

Stephen Dillane is remarkable as the lonely Wiesler, who begins by giving dry, bureaucratic reports (Dreyman and Sieland end one evening “having intercourse, presumably”), but, as he connects with them, he grows physically ravaged by this morally corrosive work.

In a live theatrical setting, that becomes irresistibly compelling. Leading the cast are Keira Knightley as Christa-Maria Sieland and Luke Thompson as Georg Dreyman. They make a compelling duo, portraying a loving couple whose relationship gradually bristles with nervous energy as suspicion, pressure and betrayal creep in.
A must watch in the West End this year!
The Lives of Others is a fascinating, urgent and thought-provoking watch that looks back at history while being unafraid to draw comparisons to more recent events.
I thought it was an absolutely superb production, a fantastic adaptation of a really good film, and I'm giving it a big fat five stars ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️.

cn.t: Robert Icke's stylish adaptation dazzles with technical stagecraft and strong performances, particularly from Knightley, but critics are divided on whether the elaborate direction overwhelms the source material's subtlety.

lo.inst: Draws Mondays at 11 AM via TodayTix app only.
